hints: Remember temperature affects rate and equilibrium position in two different ways, so think about them separately.
Normal Haber conditions are around 450 degrees C, so 600 degrees C is a temperature increase which gives particles more kinetic energy.
The forward reaction is exothermic with a negative $\Delta H$, so use Le Chatelier to decide which direction is favoured when it gets hotter.
walkthrough:
**Spot what changed**

Normal Haber process runs at about 450 degrees C. Here it jumped to 600 degrees C, so this is a clear temperature increase.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3$$

**Think about rate first**

Higher temperature means particles have more kinetic energy. There are more frequent and more successful collisions.

Rate rule:
$$\text{higher } T \rightarrow \text{more energy} \rightarrow \text{faster rate}$$

**Think about equilibrium yield next**

The forward reaction is exothermic, $\Delta H^{\ominus} = -92 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. By Le Chatelier, adding heat favours the endothermic direction to absorb it.

That means equilibrium shifts left, back toward $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$:
$$\text{heat favours reverse (endothermic) reaction, so yield of } \text{NH}_3 \text{ falls}$$

**Combine the two effects**

Rate and yield go opposite ways here. Ammonia is made faster to reach equilibrium, but the equilibrium position holds less ammonia.

Conclusion: formed faster, equilibrium yield decreased.

options.A: Correct. Higher temperature increases kinetic energy so the forward (and reverse) reactions speed up, ammonia appears faster. But because the forward reaction is exothermic, Le Chatelier shifts equilibrium to the left at higher T, so the equilibrium yield of $\text{NH}_3$ decreases.
options.B: Incorrect. It is right that the rate is faster, but the yield does not increase. A common trap is to think faster means more product at equilibrium. For an exothermic forward reaction, higher T shifts equilibrium away from products.
options.C: Incorrect. The yield part is right (decreased), but the rate part is wrong. Higher temperature never slows the reaction down, it always provides more energy for successful collisions, so formation is faster not slower.
options.D: Incorrect. Both parts are reversed. Students sometimes confuse the effect of temperature with the effect of a catalyst (which does not change yield) or mix up exothermic with endothermic. Higher T speeds up the reaction but lowers the yield for this exothermic synthesis.
